chapters.title: Not Enough for Sam
chapters.text:
Deputy Sam Bramble arrived at the Rolling Pin Bakery just after closing, his hat in his hands and his boots dusted with sawdust from the village hall. Hattie set a mug of coffee and a warm apple turnover in front of him before he could say a word. Biscuit, sensing crumbs, settled hopefully on the stool beside him.

"Aunt Hattie," Sam said, "Winnie tells me you have been reading gardening books again."

Hattie opened her little green notebook and turned it toward him. She showed him the pressed foxglove leaf, the envelope of crushed leaves, the empty hook in the potting shed, and the honey that never should have been in Lionel's cup. She spoke slowly and clearly, the way she used to explain long division to restless fourth graders.

Sam listened to every word, which she appreciated. Then he rubbed the back of his neck. "It is a good story," he said gently. "Maybe even the right one. But Detective Hask will not trade Delia for a pressed leaf and a hunch. A whiff of hand cream is not evidence. I need something real, something a judge can hold in his hands."

Hattie sighed and broke a turnover in half, giving the smaller piece to Biscuit. The cat ate it with great dignity. "Then I will find you something real," she said. "Something on paper, with ink on it." Sam smiled despite himself. "That is exactly what worries me."

chapters.title: A Hand That Wasn't Delia's
chapters.text:
The next morning Hattie carried a basket of cinnamon buns across the square to the Sugar and Spoon. Delia Fairweather looked tired, but her shop smelled of butter and cardamom, and two customers were waiting at the counter. The village had kept its promise.

"I need to see your order book," Hattie said, once the customers had gone. "The one for bake-off week." Delia pulled a fat ledger from under the register and flipped to a pink order form clipped inside. "This came by mail the Friday before," she said. "A plum cake for the judges' table, delivered to the tea tent at ten sharp. Signed by me, apparently, and approved by the committee."

Hattie bent close. The form was neat and businesslike, but the signature at the bottom was wrong. It leaned to the right in tidy, careful loops, the kind a person makes when they are copying something slowly. Delia's real handwriting was a quick, cheerful scrawl that looked as if a seagull had stepped in flour.

"I never signed this," Delia whispered. "I thought the committee had chosen my cake because they liked it. I was so proud."

"Someone wanted your cake on that table at exactly that moment," Hattie said. She copied the loops into her green notebook, stroke by stroke, and tucked the pink form into an envelope. "And someone practiced writing your name to make sure of it." Delia pressed a hand to her mouth. Outside, a gull laughed on the rooftop.

chapters.title: The Cake Was Clean
chapters.text:
Sam burst into the Rolling Pin at noon, so out of breath that Biscuit leapt off the windowsill in alarm. He waved a folded sheet of paper from the county lab.

"The results came back," he said. "Aunt Hattie, you were right about the saucer. It held traces of foxglove, steeped strong, like a tea. But the plum cake was clean. Every crumb of it. Not a speck of anything but plums, sugar, and a great deal of butter."

Hattie sat down hard on the flour bin. She had believed it all along, but believing and knowing were two different things, like a list of ingredients and a finished pie.

Within the hour, Detective Lorna Hask had driven to the Sugar and Spoon herself. Hattie and Winnie watched from the bookshop window as the detective stood on the step, spoke a few brisk words, and shook Delia's hand. Delia burst into tears, and then, being Delia, she went inside and came back out with a box of lemon tarts for the detective to take home.

"She is officially cleared," Sam reported later. "Hask says the poison was in the tea, not the cake. It was given to him before he ever sat down to judge." Winnie poured three cups of cocoa to celebrate, with extra whipped cream. Hattie smiled, but her mind was already moving. If the poison was in his morning tea, then the person who poisoned him had been close enough to brew it.

chapters.title: Closed on Tuesdays
chapters.text:
Oswald Finch was shelving large-print mysteries when Hattie came into the Pennywhistle Harbor library with a bag of oatmeal cookies. The librarian accepted them with the grave delight of a man who was not supposed to eat at the circulation desk.

"I have a strange question," Hattie said. "On the morning of the bake-off, did you have many visitors?" Oswald blinked at her over his half-moon spectacles. "Visitors? Hattie, the library was closed. We are always closed on Tuesday mornings. That is when the furnace man comes, and when I take the book van out to the farms. I locked the doors at six the night before and did not open them again until two o'clock."

Hattie held very still. "Nobody could have been reading in here?" "Not unless they came down the chimney," Oswald said, pointing at the brass sign by the door. Closed Tuesday Mornings, it said, in letters large enough for a seagull to read.

Hattie thanked him, tucked her notebook into her coat pocket, and walked slowly back along Harbor Street. The wind had turned cold, and the maple leaves skittered ahead of her like mice. Someone had sat across from her and sworn they had spent that whole morning quietly reading at the library. It had been a calm, simple alibi, and she had written it down without a second thought.

Now it had crumbled like a dry pie crust. Hattie remembered exactly who had told her that.

chapters.title: An Invitation to Tea
chapters.text:
That evening Hattie sat at her kitchen table with a stack of cream-colored cards and her best fountain pen. Biscuit supervised from the top of the bread box, his tail twitching each time the pen scratched.

Winnie came over with a thermos of cocoa and read over her shoulder. "A thank-you tea," she said. "For the five people who were questioned. Hattie Bramble, that is either very kind or very sneaky."

"It can be both," Hattie said. "Everyone in this village has had a hard week. The least I can do is feed them." She wrote out each invitation by hand: Thursday at four, the Rolling Pin Bakery, scones and sandwiches and a pot of good strong tea. She addressed one to the Sugar and Spoon, one to the Gull's Rest Inn, one to the harbor office, one to the little cottage by the lighthouse, and one more to the inn for the guest who still had a room there.

Winnie raised an eyebrow. "And what will you serve?" "Lemon scones, cucumber sandwiches, and my maple shortbread," Hattie said. "And two little pots on every table. One of honey. One of lavender sugar." Winnie set down her cocoa very carefully. "Oh," she said. "Oh, my."

The next morning Hattie delivered every card herself, smiling and chatting at each door. Then she went home, baked until midnight, and set out her very best china.

chapters.title: Honey and Lavender
chapters.text:
By four o'clock on Thursday, the Rolling Pin was warm and golden and smelled of browned butter. Five guests sat at the little round tables, looking as stiff as starched napkins. Winnie poured the tea. Biscuit wove between the chair legs, collecting pats and crumbs like taxes.

Hattie moved from table to table with a plate of maple shortbread, chatting about nothing much. The weather. The harbor. The new bench by the lighthouse. Then, as she set down a fresh pot of tea, she lifted the little jar of honey and smiled.

"Poor Lionel," she said lightly. "Everyone knew he hated honey. Such a shame someone stirred it into his tea anyway. I suppose it hides a bitter taste beautifully." She turned the lavender sugar in the light. "And lavender is so lovely, isn't it? Some people use it in hand cream. It clings to everything. Even a potting shed."

The room went very quiet. Someone cleared a throat. Someone else reached for a scone and thought better of it. Then, somewhere behind her, a teacup began to rattle against its saucer, a tiny, frantic sound, like a moth caught behind glass. It went on for a long moment before a hand steadied it.

Hattie did not turn around. She did not need to. She simply offered the nearest guest another piece of shortbread and kept her face as calm as a pond. But later, washing up, she noticed that one saucer had a fresh little chip on its rim.

chapters.title: The Photograph
chapters.text:
Winnie burst into the bakery the next morning before the bell had finished jingling. She was wearing her bathrobe under her raincoat and carrying a shoebox of photographs.

"I almost forgot," she said breathlessly. "On bake-off morning I got up early to photograph the sunrise for the bookshop newsletter. I walked right past the inn. I only picked up the prints from the drugstore yesterday."

She spread them across the counter. Pink sky over the harbor. Gulls on the pilings. The white steeple of the church. And then one snapshot that made Hattie set down her rolling pin.

It showed the stone wall of the inn garden in the gray light before dawn. The little wooden gate stood open. Slipping through it, half turned away, was a figure in a long coat with a scarf pulled up high. The face was nothing but a pale blur, because Winnie had been shivering and the camera had wobbled. But the figure was small, and it was carrying something tucked tight under one arm, something that might have been a bundle of green stalks.

"The time is printed in the corner," Winnie said, tapping it. "Six fourteen. Hours before the judging." Hattie studied the blurry figure for a long time. She noticed the small, neat shoes, dark with mud, and the careful way the coat was buttoned all the way to the top. "Winnie Calloway," she said softly, "you may have just taken the most important picture in Pennywhistle Harbor."

chapters.title: The Green Notebook
chapters.text:
Long after midnight, Hattie sat at her kitchen table in her flannel nightgown with the little green notebook open in front of her. Biscuit slept in the fruit bowl, which he was not allowed to do, and she was too busy to scold him.

She tore out a fresh page for each clue and laid them out in rows, like cookies cooling on a rack. The cut foxglove in the walled garden. The empty hook where the shears should hang. The apron with its green stains. The honey in the cup of a man who hated honey. The travel kettle steaming in the Blue Suite at dawn. The train ticket from the day before anyone was expected. The recipe notebook that matched his famous book. The contract in his name alone. The letter firing someone close to him.

Then the rest. Lavender in the shed. A muddy trowel. Small muddy boots. Crushed leaves in an envelope. The saucer, the timetable, the pressed leaf, the forged order, the alibi that had crumbled, and the small figure in Winnie's photograph.

One by one, Hattie drew lines between the pages with her pencil. Who had been close enough to brew his tea? Who had known the timetable? Who had the most to lose if that letter was sent?

The lines all met in the same place. Hattie sat back and let out a long breath. The kitchen clock ticked. Biscuit opened one eye. "Yes," she told him quietly. "I know. Now I only need to prove it."

chapters.title: The Same Hand
chapters.text:
At first light Hattie fetched Delia from the Sugar and Spoon and brought her back to the Rolling Pin, where she pulled an old tin box down from the top shelf. Inside were recipe cards from the Harvest Bake-Off, each one handwritten by a contestant and kept by the committee. Gordon had given her the box weeks ago, glad to be rid of it.

But Hattie did not want the old ones. She wanted the newest card, the one slipped into the tin this year by a guest who had offered a recipe for the inn's welcome dinner. Pear and ginger tart. Hattie had admired the tidy handwriting at the time.

She laid the card on the counter beside the pink order form. Delia leaned in. So did Biscuit, who had jumped up uninvited. The loops leaned the same way. The capital letters had the same careful curl, as if each one had been drawn slowly with the tongue between the teeth. The small d had the same odd little flag at the top. Even the ink, a deep navy blue, was the same.

"It is the same hand," Delia breathed. "Hattie, whoever wrote this card forged my name."

Hattie nodded. She photographed both pages and called Sam, who came at once. He studied them for a long minute, and then he looked up at his aunt with something new in his eyes. "That," he said, "is something a judge can hold."

chapters.title: Sunset in the Garden
chapters.text:
By evening, everyone had come. Sam had asked them politely, and Detective Lorna Hask had asked them less politely, and so the whole party gathered in the walled garden of the Gull's Rest Inn as the sunset spilled red and gold across the harbor.

The air smelled of woodsmoke and wet leaves. The last roses hung heavy on the wall, and the tall foxglove stalks still standing glowed purple in the long light. Dottie Quill stood by the potting shed with her arms folded. Oswald Finch had come, and Abe Tolliver too, his cap pulled low, because no one in Pennywhistle Harbor wanted to miss this. Winnie held Biscuit, who for once was not squirming.

Hattie stepped onto the flagstone path with her green notebook in one hand. She walked them through it slowly, the way she used to walk a classroom through a hard sum. The foxglove. The empty hook. The kettle at dawn. The honey he hated. The pressed leaf. The library that had been closed. The blurry figure at the gate. The handwriting that matched, loop for loop. Detective Hask said nothing, but she had stopped tapping her foot.

The sun touched the sea. A gull called once from the lighthouse. Five faces watched Hattie, and one of them had gone very pale. Hattie closed her notebook. She took a breath, lifted her chin, and raised her hand to point.

If you have gathered every clue, dear reader, turn now to the Final Reveal and find the name for yourself.

epilogue.title: Epilogue: Tea and Truth
epilogue.text:
The name was Colette Marsh. For twelve years she had brewed Lionel's tea, typed his letters, and quietly invented the recipes that made him famous. Then he signed a contract for her newest cookbook under his own name alone and drafted a letter firing her. When she found it, something in her went cold.

Her early train ticket showed she had arrived a day ahead of everyone, time enough to study the walled garden and cut the foxglove herself. On bake-off morning she steeped the leaves in her travel kettle, poured the tea into his monogrammed teacup, and stirred in honey to hide the bitterness. Weeks before, she had forged Delia's signature on a cake order, so that when Lionel faltered at the tasting table, everyone would blame the plum cake. Faced with the photograph and the matching handwriting, Colette did not argue. She folded her hands, and Detective Hask led her quietly away through the garden gate.

Delia was cleared, and by Monday the Sugar and Spoon was busier than ever. Detective Hask came to the Rolling Pin with a sincere apology and bought two pies. Sam told everyone at the station that his aunt was the finest detective in Maine, and Biscuit was given a whole sardine on a china saucer.

The Harvest Bake-Off was held again the following Saturday. Hattie's apple pie won the blue ribbon, but she gave the prize money to Delia and put the kettle on for everyone.
